public_rationale: The sentence is mainly a causal claim about market psychology. It says the 'companies will build their own software' story took hold because it flattered a pro-AI bias, and that this moved stocks. The stock moves did happen: a software index fell about 25% after Claude Cowork launched. But the speaker gives no way to test why investors believed the story. 'Nobody is building their own SAP or Salesforce or Office 365' is plain hyperbole with no threshold. Partial cases like Klarna's internal stack or Cursor replacing a small CMS neither prove nor disprove it. Scoring it would mean inventing a threshold and a measure of bias that he did not supply, so I do not score it.
limitations: Other readers might treat 'nobody' as a checkable factual premise. Even then, evidence on whole-suite replacements is anecdotal.
The context items describe the selloff and example cases. They do not measure investor motives.

'Nobody' is plainly rhetorical. It means no meaningful trend of replacing whole SAP, Salesforce or Office 365 suites, not literally zero companies. One or two partial examples would not test it fairly.
'Some stocks went up and some stocks went down' is trivially true and adds nothing to test.
criteria.support_condition: Not scorable. It would need a measurable test of why investors adopted the story, plus a defined threshold for 'nobody'. The speaker gave neither.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Not scorable for the same reasons. A broad, documented trend of large companies replacing whole SAP, Salesforce or Office 365 suites with in-house builds would undercut the premise. Isolated partial cases would not.
